item.title: 17-year-old questioned over alleged temple theft in Howell Road
item.description: A 17 year old boy is being questioned in relation to an alleged case of sacrilege whereby money was stolen from a temple in Howell Road yesterday morning. Police say the matter was reported yesterday morning.
item.content:encoded:
A 17 year old boy is being questioned in relation to an alleged case of sacrilege whereby money was stolen from a temple in Howell Road yesterday morning.

Police say the matter was reported yesterday morning.

A temple committee member told fijivillage News that $2,000 was stolen among other items.

We have also received information that the juvenile was also involved in another temple break in in Nasinu two weeks ago, we are following up with Police regarding this.

The juvenile is currently in custody at the Samabula Police Station as investigations continue.

item.title: Government reviews 26 iTaukei laws as Opposition raises concerns about uncertainty
item.description: Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga says its review of laws affecting iTaukei land, resources and traditional institutions is aimed at strengthening rights and correcting past concerns, while Opposition MP Jone Usamate says any changes must be based on truth and goodwill and should clearly benefit iTaukei people. While delivering his ministerial statement, Turaga says 26 laws introduced between
item.content:encoded:
Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga says its review of laws affecting iTaukei land, resources and traditional institutions is aimed at strengthening rights and correcting past concerns, while Opposition MP Jone Usamate says any changes must be based on truth and goodwill and should clearly benefit iTaukei people.

While delivering his ministerial statement, Turaga says 26 laws introduced between 2007 and 2022 had been identified for review, with nine already repealed, amended or superseded.

Turaga says the Government's approach is anchored in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and that reforms must be undertaken through consultation and within Fiji's constitutional and legal framework.

While responding in the iTaukei language, Usamate says Opposition MPs are ready to assist with the review but questioned the need for changes that could create fear or uncertainty among iTaukei communities.

He says no iTaukei land was sold between 2007 and 2022 and highlighted developments during the period, including improved access to electricity and water, bridge construction and changes to the administration of iTaukei land and lease money.

Usamate is urging the Government to ensure any changes to existing laws preserve measures that have benefited iTaukei people.

He also welcomed the re-establishment of the Great Council of Chiefs but called on the Government not to politicise chiefs and traditional leaders.

Turaga then says Government will not trade one injustice for another and that reforms must address legitimate grievances without creating new legal uncertainty for landowners, families and communities.

He says the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Bill 2025 is before the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights, while work is also progressing on the Traditional Knowledge and Cultural Expressions Bill.

Turaga adds that the Constitutional Reform Commission had completed its nationwide consultations and is finalising its report for submission to the President on the 31st of this month.

item.title: U.S citizen accused of US$165M Ponzi scheme deported from Fiji
item.description: A U.S citizen accused of running an alleged Ponzi scheme worth more than US$165 million has been deported from Fiji to the United States to face federal charges. The U.S Embassy in Fiji confirm Edward Zimbardi was deported on Friday following cooperation between Fiji’s Ministry of Immigration, the Fiji Police Force and U.S. authorities.
item.content:encoded:
A U.S citizen accused of running an alleged Ponzi scheme worth more than US$165 million has been deported from Fiji to the United States to face federal charges.

The U.S Embassy in Fiji confirm Edward Zimbardi was deported on Friday following cooperation between Fiji’s Ministry of Immigration, the Fiji Police Force and U.S. authorities.

Zimbardi faces federal charges of wire fraud and money laundering in connection with the alleged scheme, which reportedly victimised thousands of people.

The U.S Attorney for the Northern District of Georgia, Theodore S. Hertzberg, says Zimbardi allegedly tricked thousands of people into investing in his “Crypto Program” by promising huge returns.

Hertzberg says Zimbardi allegedly used the money for risky currency trades, payments to early investors, a house and expensive vehicles instead.

He says when the alleged scheme collapsed, Zimbardi fled to Fiji in an attempt to evade federal prosecution.

The operation to return Zimbardi to the United States involved the U.S E mbassy in Suva’s Diplomatic Security Service, the United States Department of Justice Office of International Affairs and the FBI.

Hertzberg says, with the assistance of law enforcement and diplomatic authorities in Fiji and the United States, Zimbardi has been returned to th e U.S a nd will face trial.

The U.S Emb assy in Suva has commended the Ministry of Immigration and the Fiji Police Force for their speed and proficiency in handling the case.

The allegations against Zimbardi have not been proven in court.

He will appear in federal court today to face wire fraud and money laundering charges.

item.title: FCEF challenges FTUC $8 living wage petition, calls for evidence-based approach
item.description: The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation says the Fiji Trades Union Congress campaign for an $8-an-hour national living wage must be based on evidence and proper wage-setting processes, rather than the number of signatures collected. FCEF CEO Edward Bernard says while the federation respects FTUC’s democratic right to target 100,000 signatures for its petition, a petition cannot replace a credib
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation says the Fiji Trades Union Congress campaign for an $8-an-hour national living wage must be based on evidence and proper wage-setting processes, rather than the number of signatures collected.

FCEF CEO Edward Bernard says while the federation respects FTUC’s democratic right to target 100,000 signatures for its petition, a petition cannot replace a credible wage-setting system.

Bernard's comments come following FTUC's $8-an-hour national living wage , which began last week.

Bernard says the issue is not whether workers deserve decent wages, but whether an $8-an-hour rate can be justified through evidence, economic analysis, transparent methodology and genuine tripartite dialogue.

He says a petition can show how many people support an $8 wage, but cannot determine whether Fiji is ready for a living wage or whether $8 is the appropriate benchmark.

Bernard says the International Labour Organisation has set out principles for establishing a living wage, including the use of robust evidence, consultation with workers and employers, transparency and technical validation.

He says the process should also reflect local and regional economic realities before a living wage is introduced through established wage-setting mechanisms.

Bernard says FTUC's proposal of $8 an hour national living wage represents an increase of about 60 percent and notes that the ILO's operationalisation principles refer to incremental progression from minimum wages towards living wages.
